# Perseus Defense builds $10K counter-drone missiles to fill gap between Patriot and short-range systems

Sep 10, 2025 with Jason Cornelius

## Key Points

- Perseus Defense is selling counter-drone missiles for under $10,000 per shot, undercutting Raytheon's $250,000 Coyote system while targeting the mid-range gap between short-range autocannon and $10 million Patriot missiles.
- The startup ran five design iterations and launched over 30 missiles during its 10-week YC batch, demonstrating a fire-and-forget thermal seeker system light enough for soldiers to carry in 25-missile pods.
- Perseus is bypassing traditional SBIR grant cycles by briefing multiple Pentagon offices, working with Fort Hood's First Cavalry Division for field testing, and building a pipeline of DoD supporters ahead of demo readiness.

Jason Cornelius Perseus Defense

## Summary

# U.S Firm Perseus Defense Tests 'Harpe' Low-Cost Kinetic MK-II Drone Interceptor at Yuma Proving Ground During Falcon Peak 26.2 

 Published on September 18, 2026 

YUMA, Ariz. — U.S. counter-drone startup Perseus Defense has tested its low-cost Mk-III interceptor, also known as the Harpe, during the Falcon Peak 26.2 homeland-defense experiment at the U.S. Army’s Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona.

The live-fire demonstration took place at Cibola Range Site 17 and involved U.S. Northern Command (NORTHCOM), the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), and Joint Interagency Task Force 401 (JIATF-401).

### Low-cost kinetic interceptor

The Harpe is designed as a hit-to-kill kinetic interceptor that physically strikes small drones instead of relying on electronic jamming or spoofing.

Perseus said the Mk-III costs approximately $2,500 to manufacture. The company is targeting a cost per engagement well below the $100,000-plus cost of some existing kinetic interceptors.

The interceptor is approximately 61 centimeters (24 inches) long and has a stated 2-kilometer engagement range. It is designed to engage Group 1 and Group 2 small unmanned aircraft systems.

A US defense startup has tested a low-cost interceptor missile designed to physically destroy small drones, offering the military a potentially affordable way to protect installations from aerial incursions.

Perseus Defense fired its Mk-III interceptor from an eight-shot launcher at Cibola Range Site 17 at Arizona’s Yuma Proving Ground this month. 

The demonstration formed part of Falcon Peak 26.2, a counter-small unmanned aircraft systems experiment involving US Northern Command, NORAD and the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401.

Each interceptor reportedly costs approximately $2,500 to build, according to the company. That could help address the cost imbalance created when militaries use missiles priced above $100,000 to destroy drones worth only a few hundred dollars.
